subject: MGMT160
title: Organising: Structure, Authority, Delegation and Coordination

questions.stem: Describe organising.
options: Arranging resources and assigning tasks to achieve goals — who does what, who reports to whom, how work is coordinated
Deciding what the company should achieve next year and setting the goals, budgets and timelines that will get it there
Motivating employees to work harder by communicating the vision and recognising good performance in front of the team
Checking results against the goal at the end of each month and correcting whatever has gone wrong before the next review
questions.why: Planning decides what; organising decides who and how. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Identify a problem that appears without organising.
options: Duplicated work — two people do the same task and a third task nobody does
Too many written plans, so that managers spend their time reading instead of acting
Employees working too few hours because nobody has told them how long the day should be
Managers delegating too much and losing track of what their teams are actually doing
questions.why: Without organising: confusion, duplicated work, conflict over turf and wasted time. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Describe an organisation chart.
options: The one-page map showing jobs, reporting relationships, authority and communication flow
A list of the company's products and prices, with the department responsible for each one
The building plan showing where each office is and which teams sit next to each other
A record of employees' salaries, grades and job titles kept by the human resources department
questions.why: The chart answers: where am I, who is my boss, who are my teammates. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe the chain of command.
options: The line of authority from the top to every employee, along which orders, questions and problems travel
The list of the company's suppliers in the order in which they must be paid each month
The order in which employees joined the company, which decides who is promoted first
The sequence of steps for making a product, from raw materials to the finished item
questions.why: Café: employee → shift supervisor → branch manager → operations director. No skipping, no confusion. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Differentiate authority from responsibility.
options: Authority is the right to decide; responsibility is the duty to deliver and answer for results
Authority is the duty to deliver and answer for results; responsibility is the right to decide
They are the same thing, and the chapter uses the two words to mean a manager's power
Authority belongs to employees who do the work; responsibility belongs to the managers above them
questions.why: Authority = legitimate power from the position; responsibility = obligation to complete tasks and answer for results. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Explain the golden rule about authority and responsibility.
options: They must travel together, in equal amounts
Authority should always be greater than responsibility
Responsibility should always be greater than authority
Only top managers need either
questions.why: Responsibility without authority is a blame machine; authority without responsibility is a danger machine. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Describe delegation.
options: Assigning a task to someone together with the authority needed to complete it
Giving someone a task but keeping all the authority, so that every step still needs approval
Doing every task yourself to be sure it is done right, and asking staff only for help with details
Passing the blame for results to an employee while keeping the credit when things go well
questions.why: Task without authority is not delegation; it is a trap. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Identify a decision a manager should never delegate.
options: Hiring and firing decisions
Daily supply orders
Shift swaps
Training new staff on the till
questions.why: Never delegate hiring and firing, discipline conversations, final accountability or setting the standards. See the table in §5.4.

questions.stem: Describe span of control.
options: The number of employees a manager directly leads
The number of products a company sells in each of its markets
The number of layers between the top of the chart and the frontline
The size of a manager's budget and the spending limit they may approve alone
questions.why: Narrow span = few employees, close supervision; wide span = many employees, more independence. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Differentiate centralisation from decentralisation.
options: Centralised: top managers decide; decentralised: lower managers participate in decisions
Centralised: everyone works in one office building; decentralised: the company has many buildings
Centralised: one building; decentralised: many buildings
They mean the same thing, and companies use whichever word sounds more modern to investors
questions.why: Centralisation wins consistency and control; decentralisation wins speed and local fit. Real organisations mix. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four common ways to group work (departmentalisation).
options: Function, product, geography, customer type
Planning, organising, leading, controlling
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats
Top, middle, frontline, staff
questions.why: Group by whatever differs most in your business. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's rule for choosing how to group work.
options: Group by whatever differs most in your business
Always group by function, because specialists work best with other specialists
Always group by geography, because customers in different places have different needs
Let employees choose their own group, because people work best with those they like
questions.why: Same product everywhere but different cities → geography; same city, different products → product. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Describe coordination.
options: Ensuring departments and people work together toward the same goal
Giving every employee the same job so that nobody has to depend on anyone else
Removing all departments so that the whole organisation is one team
Counting the number of employees in each department
questions.why: Coordination is the price you pay for the power of specialisation. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Identify a coordination tool from the chapter.
options: Clear handover rules and a shared dashboard everyone reads
Longer working hours so that departments have more time to talk to each other
A bigger office so that all departments sit together
Replacing the slowest department with an outside supplier that meets the deadlines
questions.why: Shared plans, cross-department meetings, shared dashboard, handover rules, one person accountable for the whole experience. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Explain what happens to structures when organisations grow.
options: They break — the chart, spans and delegation map must be redrawn
They stay the same forever, because a structure that worked once will work again
They automatically improve, because experience teaches people where to go for decisions
Only the logo and the name change, while the structure underneath remains the same
questions.why: Organising is not done once; the structure that fitted 15 people fails at 90. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the café where employees keep asking 'who should we report to?' and the manager says 'everyone just help each other'. Determine the problem.
options: Missing structure — nobody knows who does what or who their boss is
Employees are not working hard enough, so the manager has to encourage them to help each other
The café has too many customers for the number of staff, so everyone is confused
The manager is too strict, so employees are afraid to take decisions without asking
questions.why: Nobody complains about working hard; everyone complains about working blind. See the answer to question 1 in §5.1.

questions.stem: Analyse an employee told 'campaign first' by the marketing manager and 'client first' by the sales manager the same morning. Determine the fix.
options: Unity of command — one boss per person; the two managers agree the priority, she does not referee it
Let the employee choose which boss to obey, since she knows the work best
Give the employee a third boss who decides between the other two whenever they disagree
Tell the employee to do both at once and to work extra hours if the day is not long enough
questions.why: Two bosses create conflicting priorities and the employee gets blamed for both. See the answer to question 3 in §5.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'approve discounts up to AED 200'.
options: Authority
Responsibility
Coordination
Control
questions.why: The right to decide and use resources is authority. See Exercise 1 and §5.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'answer for this month's customer-satisfaction score'.
options: Responsibility
Authority
Span of control
Centralisation
questions.why: The duty to deliver and answer for results is responsibility. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a supervisor blamed for satisfaction scores she has no power to fix. Determine the chapter's name for this.
options: Responsibility without authority — the blame machine
Authority without responsibility — the danger machine
Good delegation
A wide span of control
questions.why: Authority and responsibility must travel together in equal amounts. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the manager who answers every customer and approves every order, works twelve hours, and whose two best employees resigned saying 'no room to grow'. Determine what went wrong.
options: She confused doing everything with being responsible for everything — she failed to delegate
She delegated too much, so her employees felt overloaded and left for easier jobs
Her employees were lazy and used 'no room to grow' as an excuse for leaving
She needed a bigger office and more staff to handle the volume of customers and orders
questions.why: Delegate the task, the authority and a clear standard; keep the accountability. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Select the task a branch manager should delegate.
options: Daily supply orders and shift swaps
A discipline conversation with a staff member
Deciding whom to hire
Setting the quality standards for the café
questions.why: Routine decisions and learnable tasks are delegated; hiring, discipline and standards stay. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Select the right span of control for a hospital ICU.
options: Narrow — complex, risky work where mistakes are expensive
Wide — routine, well-trained work where staff can be left to get on with it
No manager is needed, because ICU doctors and nurses are highly trained professionals
The same as the checkout line in a supermarket, because both run on standard procedures
questions.why: Narrow spans fit complex, risky or new work; wide spans fit routine trained work like the general ward. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Classify a fast-food chain that decides menu, prices and recipes at head office but lets branches do their own hiring and local promotions.
options: A mix — centralised for consistency, decentralised for speed and local fit
Fully centralised, because head office controls the things customers notice most
Fully decentralised, because the branches make their own hiring and promotion decisions
No structure, because the two halves of the business contradict each other
questions.why: Real organisations mix: centralise the menu, decentralise hiring and promotions. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Analyse employees who say 'they asked us, then ignored us'. Determine the problem.
options: Participation without real influence breeds cynicism
Too much decentralisation, so employees expect to decide things that are not theirs to decide
A span of control that is too narrow, so managers have time to ask questions they do not need to ask
Too many departments, so the answers get lost before they reach the person who decides
questions.why: Involve people where they hold real knowledge and commitment matters — but participation must have real influence. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Select the grouping for a coffee chain with identical menus across five emirates.
options: By geography — places differ, so local teams win
By product — each drink line should own its results from bean to cup
By customer type — students, office workers and tourists want different things
By function only — all baristas, all cashiers and all supervisors in separate departments
questions.why: Same product everywhere but different places → geography. See §5.6 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Select the grouping for a company selling to individuals, corporates and government.
options: By customer type — customer needs differ more than products do
By geography — each emirate should have its own team for all three customer groups
By product — each product line should serve all three customer groups itself
By function — sales, marketing and service should each serve all three groups
questions.why: When customer needs differ most, group by customer. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Select the grouping for a firm with a coffee line and a bakery line in the same city.
options: By product — each line owns its results end to end
By geography — the coffee and bakery teams should be split by district of the city
By customer type — breakfast customers and lunch customers differ more than the lines do
By span of control — the manager with the most staff should run both lines
questions.why: Same city, very different products → product. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Analyse the hotel where reception, housekeeping and food services must hand over a room in ninety minutes and the guest walks into a dirty room. Determine the cause.
options: A coordination failure — a verbal, late or assumed handover
Too many employees involved, so each one assumed another had finished the job
The guest arrived too early, before the ninety-minute handover window had closed
A pricing error, because the room rate did not include enough time for cleaning
questions.why: Three departments, one guest: if any handover is verbal, late or assumed, work falls between the chairs. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Analyse the founder of a 90-person company who still approves every purchase, discount and schedule change, while two managers quit as 'managers in title only'. Determine the prescription.
options: Delegate decision rights by money threshold, keep hiring, pricing and brand at the top, publish the new chart, replace daily approval with a weekly dashboard
Hire more managers who also wait for the founder's approval, so that the queue of decisions is shared between more people and moves faster
Reduce the company back to 15 people, the size at which the founder's way of working was effective, and grow again more slowly
Ask the founder to work longer hours and to approve decisions in the evening, so that managers are not kept waiting during the day
questions.why: Extreme centralisation that fitted 15 broke at 90; the founder became the bottleneck. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between planning and organising.
options: Planning decides what to achieve; organising decides who does it and how
Planning is for small firms with few staff; organising is for big firms with many departments
They are the same function, described from the manager's and the employee's point of view
Organising comes before planning, because you must know who is available before you set goals
questions.why: Planning = what; organising = who and how. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Describe what employees experience when nothing is organised.
options: Confusion about who does what, duplicated work and conflict over turf
Clear roles and fast decisions, because nobody has to wait for a manager
More free time, because nobody checks whether the work is done
Higher pay, because employees negotiate their own jobs directly with the owner
questions.why: Without organising people work blind. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Identify the three questions an organisation chart answers for an employee.
options: Where am I, who is my boss, who are my teammates
How much do I earn, when is lunch, where is the car park
What is the mission, vision and goal
Who are the customers, suppliers and investors
questions.why: The chart maps position, reporting line and team. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe what the lines on an organisation chart show.
options: Reporting relationships and the flow of authority and communication
Friendships between staff
The building's corridors and which offices are connected to each other
The order in which people were hired and how long each has been with the firm
questions.why: Lines show who reports to whom. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter calls the organisation chart a one-page map.
options: It shows all the jobs and reporting lines of the organisation on one page
It shows the location of every office in the building and who sits where
It replaces the need for managers, because everyone can see what they should do
It lists every employee's salary so that pay differences are open to all
questions.why: The chart is a map of jobs, lines and authority. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe what travels along the chain of command.
options: Orders downward, and questions and problems upward
Only salaries, which are decided at the top and paid out at the bottom
Only customer complaints, which travel upward until someone solves them
Only written rules, which are issued by head office and read on the frontline
questions.why: Orders, questions and problems move along the chain. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Describe what a manager keeps when delegating properly.
options: The final accountability for the result
Nothing — the task leaves completely and the manager no longer needs to think about it
The authority, but not the task, so that every decision still comes back for approval
The daily routine work, which the manager continues to do personally
questions.why: Delegate the task, the authority and a clear standard; keep the accountability. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Explain why managers who never delegate harm their teams.
options: Employees have no room to grow and the best ones leave
Employees get too much free time, because the manager does all the interesting work
Delegation is required by employment law, so a manager who never delegates can be fined
Customers prefer dealing with the manager, so employees never build their own relationships
questions.why: Two best employees resigned saying 'no room to grow'. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Describe a narrow span of control.
options: A manager leads only a few people with close supervision
A manager leads many people with little supervision and a lot of independence
A manager with no team of their own
A company with no managers at all, in which teams supervise themselves
questions.why: Narrow span = few employees, close supervision. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify what decentralisation wins.
options: Speed and local fit
Consistency and control
Lower salaries
Fewer managers
questions.why: Decentralisation wins speed and local fit; centralisation wins consistency and control. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Describe grouping by function.
options: Putting people with the same specialism together, such as all accountants in one department
Grouping people by the city or region in which they work
Grouping people by the product line they make or sell
Grouping people by the type of customer they serve
questions.why: Function = same specialism together. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Describe grouping by product.
options: Each product line owns its own results end to end
All marketing staff sit together in one department serving every line
Teams are split by emirate, with each emirate selling the full range
Teams are split by customer size, from individuals to large corporates
questions.why: Product grouping gives each line full ownership. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Explain why specialisation needs coordination.
options: Specialised departments only create value when their work joins up for the customer
Specialists never make mistakes, so coordination is needed only for the generalists
Coordination replaces specialisation once the organisation has grown large enough
Specialists do not need managers, so coordination is how the organisation controls them
questions.why: Coordination is the price of specialisation. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Describe the idea of one person accountable for the whole experience.
options: A single owner who follows the customer across departments so nothing falls between the chairs
Every department has its own boss who answers for that department's part of the work
The customer manages the process by telling each department what the previous one did
Nobody is accountable, because the whole experience is the result of everybody's work
questions.why: One accountable person stops work falling between the chairs. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's advice for a growing company.
options: Redraw the chart, spans and delegation map as the company grows
Keep the founder approving everything, so that quality and culture are protected during growth
Hire managers in title only, so that staff have someone to report to without changing who decides
Stop growing once the structure that fitted the original team starts to show strain
questions.why: Organising is not done once. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Explain why the founder of a 90-person company becomes a bottleneck.
options: Every decision waits for one person who cannot handle them all
Founders are lazy once the company is established
Employees refuse to decide because they fear being blamed for mistakes
The company has too few customers to justify more than one decision-maker
questions.why: Extreme centralisation that fitted 15 people broke at 90. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Identify a sign that a structure has broken.
options: Managers quit saying they are managers in title only
Profits are rising faster than headcount
Customers are happy and the review scores are improving
The chart is published and every employee has a copy of it
questions.why: Managers without real authority are a sign the structure is broken. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a new restaurant where two waiters take the same table while another table waits. Determine the missing function.
options: Organising — no clear assignment of who does what
Planning — no goal for the number of tables
Controlling — no measurement of how long each table waits
Leading — no motivation, so the waiters compete for the easy tables
questions.why: Duplicated work and missed tasks are organising failures. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Select the organising action that fixes 'nobody knows who to report to'.
options: Publish a simple chart with one boss per person
Raise salaries so that employees are willing to work without clear direction
Hold a motivation speech so that employees feel part of one team
Set a sales target so that everyone knows what the business is trying to achieve
questions.why: Structure answers who reports to whom. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's view of a manager who says 'everyone just helps each other'.
options: It is missing structure — people complain about working blind, not about working hard
It is ideal teamwork, because the staff share the work without waiting for orders
It is good delegation, because the manager has handed the work to the team
It is a wide span of control, because the manager supervises everyone lightly
questions.why: Nobody complains about working hard; everyone complains about working blind. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's name for giving someone a task without the authority to complete it.
options: A trap, not delegation
Good delegation, because the manager keeps control of the decisions
Coordination, because the task is shared between the manager and the employee
Decentralisation, because the task has moved down the chart
questions.why: Task without authority is a trap. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Select the correct way to delegate the weekly supply order.
options: Give the task, the authority to order up to a limit, and a clear standard; keep accountability
Give the task but approve every item yourself before the order is sent to the supplier
Give the task and never check it again, because checking shows a lack of trust
Give the task to three people at once so that someone is always available to do it
questions.why: Task + authority + standard, keep accountability. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Select the right span of control for a call centre of well-trained agents doing routine calls.
options: Wide
Narrow
None
One agent per manager
questions.why: Routine trained work fits a wide span. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Select the grouping for a bank that serves students, families and large companies very differently.
options: By customer type
By geography
By product
By function
questions.why: Customer needs differ most. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Select the coordination tool for three departments that keep blaming each other.
options: A shared dashboard and clear handover rules
Longer hours so that the departments have more time to resolve their disputes
A bigger office so that the three departments can sit together on one floor
Replacing the slowest department with an outside supplier that meets its deadlines
questions.why: Shared plans, handover rules and one accountable person coordinate. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a patient who was discharged without medicine because the ward thought the pharmacy would deliver it and the pharmacy thought the ward would collect it. Determine the failure.
options: Coordination — an assumed handover
Span of control — the ward manager had too many nurses to supervise
Delegation — the pharmacist delegated the delivery without the authority to do so
Departmentalisation — the ward and the pharmacy are grouped by the wrong principle
questions.why: Assumed hand-offs let work fall between the chairs. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Determine the first fix for a hotel where rooms are handed over late between housekeeping and reception.
options: Write a clear handover rule with a time and an owner
Hire more receptionists so that someone is always free to check the rooms
Lower the room price so that guests complain less when the room is late
Close the restaurant so that housekeeping staff can concentrate on the rooms
questions.why: Handover rules are a coordination tool. See §5.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a company of 60 where every purchase still needs the founder's signature. Determine the fix.
options: Delegate decision rights by money threshold and replace daily approvals with a weekly dashboard
Hire a second founder who shares the signing duty so that the queue moves twice as fast
Stop all purchases until the founder has time to review the purchasing policy
Ask staff to work longer hours so that purchases can be prepared before the founder arrives
questions.why: Delegate by threshold; keep the big decisions at the top. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Select the decisions the chapter says should stay at the top as a company grows.
options: Hiring, pricing and brand
Daily supply orders from regular suppliers
Shift swaps between members of the same team
Small discounts offered to regular customers
questions.why: Keep hiring, pricing and brand at the top. See §5.8.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's reason for publishing a new chart after reorganising.
options: So everyone knows the new roles and reporting lines
To impress investors with a professional-looking organisation
Because the law requires companies above a certain size to publish their structure
To replace delegation, since a published chart tells everyone what to do
questions.why: A published chart makes the new structure real. See §5.8.
